content.title: About
content.content: Grape leaves are the edible leaves of the grapevine (Vitis vinifera), widely used in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Caucasian, and Central Asian cooking. They have a slightly tangy, earthy flavor and a tender texture when cooked. Fresh or brined, they are best known as the wrapper for stuffed dishes such as dolma, sarma, and tolma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed grape leaves are known as dolma, sarma, or tolma, depending on the country.
Young, tender leaves picked in spring are the best for cooking.
Grape leaves are sold fresh, in brine in jars, or frozen.
Brined leaves should be rinsed well to remove the salty brine.
Grape leaves have been used in cooking for thousands of years in the regions where grapes are grown.

items.title: Provides vitamin K and vitamin A
items.content: Grape leaves provide vitamin K for normal blood clotting and carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and manganese
items.content: These nutrients support the immune system and metabolism.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Grape leaves contribute fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Grape leaves contain plant compounds such as quercetin with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Grape leaves are low in calories, though stuffed dishes may be higher.

items.title: Sodium in brined leaves
items.content: Brined grape leaves can be very high in sodium, so rinse them well and check labels.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Grape leaves contain vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Oxalates and tannins
items.content: Grape leaves contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit, and tannins that may reduce iron absorption.

items.title: Residues and allergies
items.content: Wash fresh leaves thoroughly, and avoid leaves from vines that may have been sprayed. Allergic reactions are possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grape leaves are rinsed, softened by blanching if fresh, and used to wrap fillings of rice, herbs, and meat, then simmered until tender. They can also be added to pickles or used to wrap fish before grilling. Serve stuffed leaves warm or cold with yogurt or lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh grape leaves in the refrigerator in a bag for several days, or blanch and freeze them. Keep unopened brined leaves in a cool, dry place and refrigerate them in their brine after opening, using them within a few weeks. Cooked stuffed leaves should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days.
